Post-patch verification for CVE-2026-6322 in OpenShift Container Platform


An upgrade ticket can close before the risk is gone. CVE-2026-6322 affects OpenShift Container Platform and the fast-uri package that applications can bundle independently. Verification needs two tracks: the platform release and the workload image.
The vulnerability allows percent-encoded authority delimiters in a host to be decoded during normalization and emitted as raw separators. A later parser can then interpret a different host. A host allowlist, redirect validator, or outbound router that trusts the normalized authority can be bypassed.
Red Hat lists OpenShift Container Platform 4.20, 4.21, and 4.22 as affected. The fixed releases are 4.20.27, 4.21.22, and 4.22.3. Confirm the cluster version after the suppor…

The error looks like this, and it always stops the script on the spot:
PHP Fatal error:  Allowed memory size of 33554432 bytes exhausted (tried to allocate 33554440 bytes) in /var/www/app/report.php on line 3

The quick fix is to raise memory_limit. The better fix is to find out why the script needs that much memory, because in most cases it is holding something it could have processed piece by piece. Here is how to read the message, raise the limit properly, and cut the memory use itself.
Allowed memory size of 33554432 bytes is your memory_limit in bytes. Divide by 1,048,576: this one is 32 MB.
tried to allocate 33554440 bytes is the single allocation that failed, not the total used. A big number here usually means one large array or string being created or grown. PHP arrays resize by do…

articles.author: Oleksandr
articles.description:
As developers, we love optimizing our tech stack. We build custom CI/CD pipelines, configure Neovim from scratch, and spend hours tweaking our terminal themes. We understand the principles of good software architecture: separation of concerns, loose coupling, and high cohesion.
But when it comes to personal productivity, we often fall into the same trap: We build a monolith.
I used to have a productivity system that was a massive, tightly coupled monolith. I had a Notion dashboard with 47 different databases. My "Tasks" database was linked to my "Projects" database, which was linked to my "Life Areas" database.
It had a beautiful UI. And it was a nightmare to maintain.
The Monolith Problem
This is the equivalent of refactoring a 10,000-line legacy codebase just to change a button color. Your brain (the CPU) gets exhausted before you even start doing the actual work.
The Microservice Approach to Productivity
Single Responsibility Principle


Loose Coupling


Statelessness



How I Implemented It
I also implemented the "3-Task Rule". Every morning, I pull exactly three tasks from my backlog into my "Today" view. No matter how big the project is, I only see three things. It’s the ultimate way to reduce context switching and avoid decision paralysis.
The Result
If you are struggling with burnout or just feeling overwhelmed by your own productivity system, try treating it like a microservice. Refactor it. Delete the unnecessary dependencies. Make it boring.
If you want a head start, I actually built a minimalist Notion template that implements this exact 3-task architecture without any of the bloat. You can check out the ADHD Daily Planner here.
Or, if you want to read more about why over-engineered systems fail, check out this article on my blog.
articles.title: Why Developers Should Treat Their Personal Productivity Like a Microservice

articles.author: Jin Xu
articles.description:
At one point my phone had a calendar app, a budgeting app, a habit tracker, a notes app, a password manager, a mood journal and a shopping list app. Each wanted its own account. Three wanted a subscription. All of them wanted my data on their servers.
So I built LifeDesk, a single app that covers all of that and more. I gave myself one hard rule: no backend. No LifeDesk account, no LifeDesk server, nothing to breach. This post covers what that rule forced me to figure out.
Everything lives in one SQLite file on the device (expo-sqlite, WAL mode). Onboarding asks for one thing, your name, and even that never leaves the phone.
This changes a lot. Without a server there's no "fix it in the API": every bug fix that touches data has to ship as a client migration and run correctly on thousands o…
articles.title: Shipping a Privacy-First "Super App" With Expo SDK 57, SQLite and Zero Servers
